outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace

args.reason: Inspect src/timing.js and briefly compare debounce with throttling.

outcomes.prose:
`debounce(fn, wait)` delays calling `fn` until no calls have occurred for `wait` milliseconds. Each new call cancels and restarts the timer, and only the latest arguments are used.

Use it when you want one action after activity settles—for example:

- Search input: request results after the user stops typing
- Window resizing: recalculate layout after resizing ends
- Autosave: save after edits pause

Use throttling instead when you need periodic updates during continuous activity, such as updating scroll position or handling mouse movement at a limited rate.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
**What it does:** `debounce(fn, wait)` in `src/timing.js` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels any pending timer and starts a new one. `fn` runs only after `wait` ms pass with no further calls, and it receives the arguments from the last call.

Some limits of this implementation:
- It is trailing-edge only, so `fn` never fires at the start of a burst.
- It has no `cancel` or `flush` method.
- It doesn't preserve `this`, because the wrapper is an arrow function.
- It returns nothing to the caller.

**Debounce vs. throttle:**
- **Debounce:** use it when only the final value of a burst matters. It waits for the activity to stop. Typical cases are:
  - search-as-you-type requests
  - autosave after typing stops
  - validating a field once the user pauses
  - recalculating layout after a window resize ends
- **Throttle:** use it when you need regular updates during continuous activity. It runs at most once per interval while events keep coming. Typical cases are:
  - scroll or drag handlers
  - mousemove tracking
  - progress or analytics pings
  - game or animation input

Under constant events, a debounced function may never fire, while a throttled one fires every interval.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] A one-line question gets a one-line answer
outcomes.prose: HTTP 418 means "I'm a teapot." It comes from RFC 2324, the Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol, an April Fools' joke from 1998. A teapot returns it when it's asked to brew coffee. The code isn't meant for real use, but some servers return it anyway as an Easter egg. Some also use it to turn away unwanted requests, such as bot traffic.
